meta.ogDescription: Not Red Auerbach. James Howell printed it in 1655 as “the whole Land of promise” — the modern wording is a 19th-century newspaper mutation.

answer.label: Not Red Auerbach — actually James Howell
answer.authorDates: c. 1594 – c. 1666 · Anglo-Welsh writer & first Historiographer Royal
answer.sourceLine: The line is Howell’s, printed in 1655 in his Epistolae Ho-Elianae as “An acre of performance is worth the whole Land of promise.” The familiar sports-page wording — “a whole world of promise” — is a 19th-century newspaper mutation, and Red Auerbach was quoting a proverb that had already been in circulation for three centuries.
answer.confidenceText: Origin documented by Quote Investigator to a 1655 printed letter; the Auerbach version is a later variant.

source.excerpt: An acre of performance is worth the whole Land of promise; Besides, as the Italian hath it, Deeds are men, and words women.
trail: 1655 — James Howell prints “An acre of performance is worth the whole Land of promise” in the fourth volume of his Epistolae Ho-Elianae, per Quote Investigator ↗.

1874–1890 — American papers reshape it: a Pittsburgh paper has “a whole world full of promise” in 1874, and an 1890 Arkansas Democrat aphorism column prints “the whole world of promise” credited to “Howells” — one step from the modern wording, as documented by QI ↗.
1911–1924 — the line is openly assigned to novelist W. D. Howells, from an Asbury Park literature column to a Philadelphia furniture advertisement (QI ↗).

2006 — a Washington Times sports-section obituary by Dick Heller quotes Red Auerbach with “a whole world of promise”; QI notes he “may have employed an instance after it had been circulating for a few hundred years” (source ↗).
source.excerptNote: Wording as transcribed by Quote Investigator from the 1655 printing; 17th-century capitalisation retained.

source.rightsNote: Howell’s letter was first published in London in 1655, and the reworded American newspaper versions date from 1874–1911 — all far earlier than 1931, so the text is in the public domain in the United States. Only modern editorial matter (introductions, notes) in later editions could carry its own copyright.

author.name: James Howell
author.heading: Who was James Howell?
author.metaLine: c. 1594 – c. 1666 · Anglo-Welsh letter-writer & first Historiographer Royal
author.bio: James Howell was a Welsh-born writer who spent years travelling Europe on business for a London glass factory before politics landed him in the Fleet Prison in the 1640s. There he assembled Epistolae Ho-Elianae (“Howell’s Letters”), a collection of familiar letters — some genuine, some almost certainly composed for the page — that became one of the first books in English to make its author a living by his pen. In 1660 Charles II appointed him the first Historiographer Royal.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Two other names carry this line today — and one of the swaps came down to a single missing letter.

items.why: Quote sites list it with no citation. The earliest Auerbach-linked instance Quote Investigator documents ↗ is a 2006 Washington Times sports-section obituary by Dick Heller — the saying was already in print by 1655.

An 1890 aphorism column in the Arkansas Democrat printed it “—Howells,” and by 1911 a New Jersey paper was crediting “W. D. Howells”; QI concludes the ascription came from confusion between ‘Howell’ and ‘Howells’ ↗.

Howell wrote “the whole Land of promise.” An 1874 Pittsburgh paper had “a whole world full of promise,” by 1890 the Arkansas Democrat had “the whole world of promise” — one step from the “a whole world of promise” that Auerbach used.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence belongs to James Howell, printed in 1655 — as Quote Investigator concluded ↗: he “should be credited with the quotation he wrote that was published in 1655.”

context.heading: Why the wording drifted
lead: The saying travelled a long way before it reached a basketball bench. Howell’s 1655 version puns on scripture: an acre you actually farm beats the whole Land of promise you have merely been pledged. Somewhere in the 19th-century newspaper filler trade the biblical “Land” softened into a generic “world,” and the pun quietly died.

The attribution wandered too. An 1890 aphorism column in the Arkansas Democrat credited it to “Howells” — one letter off — and the novelist and Atlantic Monthly editor William Dean Howells inherited the line for a generation, according to Quote Investigator ↗. Auerbach’s no-nonsense contract-talk reputation made him the next natural host.
detailsBody: Howell’s own sentence continues with a second proverb: “Besides, as the Italian hath it, Deeds are men, and words women.” The modern quote sites keep only the first half.

No collection of Auerbach’s own writing has been shown to originate the line; the earliest citation tying it to him that Quote Investigator records is a 2006 Washington Times sports-section obituary by Dick Heller.
context.pull: An acre you actually plough beats a whole Land you were merely promised.
